title: Cytoskeletal microdifferentiation: A mechanism for organizing morphological plasticity in dendrites

venue.name: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

abstract: Experimental evidence suggests that microfilaments and microtubules play contrasting roles in regulating the balance between motility and stability in neuronal structures. Actin-containing microfilaments are associated with structural plasticity, both during development when their dynamic activity drives the exploratory activity of growth cones and after circuit formation when the actin-rich dendritic spines of excitatory synapses retain a capacity for rapid changes in morphology. By contrast, microtubules predominate in axonal and dendritic processes, which appear to be morphologically relatively more stable. To compare the cytoplasmic distributions and dynamics of microfilaments and microtubules we made time-lapse recordings of actin or the microtubule-associated protein 2 tagged with green fluorescent protein in neurons growing in dispersed culture or in tissue slices from transgenic mice. The results complement existing evidence indicating that the high concentrations of actin present in dendritic spines is a specialization for morphological plasticity. By contrast, microtubule-associated protein 2 is limited to the shafts of dendrites where time-lapse recordings show little evidence for dynamic activity. A parallel exists between the partitioning of microfilaments and microtubules in motile and stable domains of growing processes during development and between dendrite shafts and spines at excitatory synapses in established neuronal circuits. These data thus suggest a mechanism, conserved through development and adulthood, in which the differential dynamics of actin and microtubules determine the plasticity of neuronal structures.

Short impact summary

Cytoskeletal microdifferentiation: A mechanism for organizing morphological plasticity in dendrites (2001) in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. 126 citations.

Full narrative

Cytoskeletal microdifferentiation: A mechanism for organizing morphological plasticity in dendrites (2001) in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences is authored by Stefanie Kaech, Hema Parmar and Martijn Roelandse. Topics: Microtubule, Microfilament, Biology, Cell biology and Dendritic spine.

126 citations (OpenAlex). Citations peaked in 2006 with 13 citing works. Citing venues include Journal of Neuroscience, Journal of Biological Chemistry and Neuron.

Limited online visibility beyond citations.
narrative_llm:
Short impact summary

This 2001 Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences article has sustained scholarly influence, with 126 citations in OpenAlex, 127 documented downstream reuses, and 9 scite statements classified as supporting. Its citation footprint is especially strong in neuroscience and cell biology venues, including Journal of Neuroscience, Journal of Biological Chemistry, Neuron, and Journal of Cell Science.

Full narrative

Kaech and colleagues addressed a foundational question in neuronal cell biology: how dendrites balance stability with the capacity for structural change. By focusing on the contrasting roles of actin-rich microfilaments and microtubules, the article helped frame dendritic morphology as a dynamic, cytoskeleton-dependent process rather than a fixed architectural state. That conceptual contribution is reflected in the paper’s enduring reuse across work on microtubules, actin remodeling, dendritic spines, and dendritic filopodia.

The citation record shows clear and continuing academic uptake. The article’s 126 OpenAlex citations are distributed across a broad span of years, and the citing literature is concentrated in core biomedical journals and reviews, suggesting that the paper has remained relevant to researchers studying neuronal structure, cytoskeletal organization, and plasticity mechanisms. The reuse graph reinforces that pattern: most downstream references are journal articles, with additional reuse in book chapters, reviews, preprints, and dissertations.

Topical signals in the citing landscape point to a wide mechanistic influence. Concepts such as neurogenesis and neuroplasticity, cellular mechanics, cellular transport, and microtubule dynamics recur in the citing literature, indicating that the paper’s framework has been absorbed into multiple lines of inquiry beyond dendritic morphology alone. The more recent citing works also show that the article continues to be used in contemporary studies of dendritic organization and microtubule behavior.

The record for public and community attention is comparatively sparse: event-data sources show no online mentions, while the archived public-discourse data do not add substantial additional reach. Even so, the scholarly footprint is substantial and well established, and the paper’s open-access availability in repository records may have helped support its long-term accessibility and reuse.
